extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in philosophy of humour, cultural criticism, and comedy (general educated public and students/scholars of philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine/essay–style philosophical analysis that examines competing theories of laughter (superiority, relief, carnival) and their cultural/political implications, with attention to contemporary comedy and online discourse. The piece situates historical theorists (Hobbes, Freud, Bakhtin, Baudelaire, Kundera, Dolar, Critchley) to evaluate whether laughter is liberating or reinforcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: True comedy as confrontation with shared lack/failure
rubrics_metrics.description: True comedy is defined by its ability to confront us with a deeply philosophical realization: that we’re all lacking, with failure at our core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy's power lies in revealing a universal human condition (failure/ lack) that connects people; loss of this universalist spirit threatens comedy's emancipatory potential. The essay urges revisiting historical philosophies of comedy to recover this function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory (secure superiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: 'laughter is nothing else but a sudden glory arising from some sudden conception of some eminency in ourselves, by comparison with the infirmities of others, or with our own formerly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter here is self-celebratory, establishing the laugher's superiority over a target. It can be a group activity that affirms one person/group over another and, per Jonathan Hall, may become a 'fascist joy'—collaborating with powerholders rather than challenging them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxious superiority (Baudelaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Baudelaire: when seeing a man fall we laugh as if to say 'Look at me! I am not falling!...' — an assertion of self that is anxious rather than secure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of superiority-laughter emphasizes the 'I' and is marked by anxious boasting; the laugh may be self-undercutting because the laugher could equally be the faller. It differs from Hobbesian secure superiority but still affirms someone over another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory / carnival laughter (liberation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud: jokes lift repression and restore lost 'primary possibilities of enjoyment.' Bakhtin: 'carnival' laughter 'is the laughter of all the people… universal in its scope; it is directed at all and everyone, including the carnival’s participants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This laughter functions as liberation: it equalizes, breaks norms, can attack power (e.g., caricature), and may embrace 'inappropriate' material. It is portrayed as joyous, democratic, and universalizing rather than affirming hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as the condition of ideology (Dolar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dolar: 'Laughter is the condition of ideology. It provides us with the distance, the very space in which ideology can take its full swing. It is only with laughter that we become ideological subjects…'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter's apparent freedom and relief can make people receptive to ideological influence; the spontaneity of laughter can mask the way it solidifies worldviews. Therefore relief and superiority theories may be entangled: even 'liberating' laughter can operate ideologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological vs diabolical laughter (Kundera)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kundera: the same external display of laughter can be either 'ideological' (supporting existing ideologies) or 'diabolical' (a dangerous comedy that produces something new).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although identical outwardly, the internal orientations differ: ideological laughter reinforces the status quo; diabolical laughter disrupts and creates novelty. This distinction cautions against treating all laughter as equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactionary humour and reinforcement of consensus (Critchley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critchley: 'it is important to recognize that not all humour is [liberating], and most of the best jokes are fairly reactionary, or at best, simply serve to reinforce social consensus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective or 'good' jokes can nonetheless function reactionarily by reinforcing prevailing social norms and consensus; evaluators should not assume comedic quality equals political radicalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary online/particularist comedy (imitative laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary jokes often 'confirm what we already believe... circulated in curated feeds to target audiences... The laughter that follows them displays a kind of Dunning-Kruger effect: self-assessment takes place in which objectivity is eschewed and the superiority of the listener is simply confirmed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-media-optimized comedy is particularist: designed for in-group sharing and affirmation rather than universalizing. This 'imitative' laughter repeats and reiterates social positions and can deepen divisiveness rather than produce shared relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes' universal aspiration despite political valence
rubrics_metrics.description: All jokes—even when they seem self-celebratory—'contain a signal of the core of our subjectivity: failure, lack, disaster, and contradiction.' Attempts to divide jokes into 'ethical' and 'unethical' miss that jokes always attempt to be universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of whether a joke supports or attacks social positions, it often gestures toward universality by revealing shared human vulnerability. Evaluations should account for this universalizing impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-funny comedy as didactic and ideological
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps it is only when it isn’t funny that comedy can be truly didactic, affirmative and ideological. A comedy that confirms what we already believe is reflective of divisive online discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comedy functions primarily as affirmation (and/or fails to be funny), it may be used deliberately as didactic or ideological messaging. Distinguish between comedy that seeks laughter for liberation and comedy employed as social/political reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about typologies of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing laughter into types (superiority vs relief) can be inadequate and may 'preclude the possibility of comedy working against the excesses of contemporary culture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomies are analytically useful but risk simplifying complex overlaps; evaluators should be wary of rigidly categorizing laughter since categories can obscure how different functions (liberation, reinforcement, ideology) interpenetrate.
